text: SOAR stands for Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response -- and the best way to understand it is to take each word on its own instead of treating it as one blurred buzzword. Everything you've learned so far, the SIEM, the dashboards, is built to detect and surface things that need attention. SOAR is built to actually do something once they are.

Orchestration connects the tools a real SOC already runs -- SIEM, EDR, threat intel, email security, ticketing -- through their APIs, so data and actions move between them automatically instead of through an analyst's clipboard. Automation then runs a defined sequence of steps without a human doing each one by hand every time. Response is the part a SIEM alone never does: taking a real action itself, not just raising an alert.

A SIEM alone detects a suspicious login, raises an alert, and waits for a human to act. Add SOAR, and the same alert can trigger an automatic check against threat intel, and if the IP comes back malicious, the SOAR platform can isolate the host itself -- the same kind of EDR response action covered earlier in this course -- with the analyst notified either way, not left waiting on the first move.

None of this is automation for its own sake. Alert volume climbs every year as a SOC adds endpoints, cloud services, and log sources, while analyst headcount grows far more slowly, if at all. That gap produces alert fatigue: too many alerts for the available analysts to review carefully, so some get rushed and some get missed entirely.

SOAR closes that gap not by adding people, but by removing the well-understood, repeatable portion of the workload from a human's plate entirely, so the same team can absorb far more volume without missing what actually needs their attention. Next: playbooks, the defined, automated sequences that make all of this concrete for a specific alert type.
